drainage.local_h: Water on a Nacogdoches hillside, and where it ends up
local: Nacogdoches is hillier than most of the towns we work in, and the streets roll down toward La Nana and Banita creeks. On a slope, rain does not sit. It picks up speed and dumps against whatever is at the bottom, usually a slab, a back patio or the low corner of a bed. That is a different problem from the flat, soggy yards around Longview. Our first job is working out where the water enters your lot and where it leaves, because the right fix depends on that.

The clay under most of East Texas stops water a foot or so down, and on a hillside that water turns sideways and travels along the slope. It can show up as a wet streak halfway down the yard, well below the roof. A swale cut across the slope above the house catches surface runoff. A French drain handles water that is trapped in the soil. We pick between them after watching where the water actually travels, and on a steep lot we often use both.

Every drain we build uses sock-wrapped 4 inch perforated pipe over #57 stone, backfilled with stone and capped with soil and sod. Each run ties to a daylighted outlet or a pop-up emitter, never a buried dead end. On a hill that part is easier, since you have fall to work with and a lower part of the lot to send water to. Downspouts get solid pipe carried well away from the house, and bare slopes get erosion control.

A wall and a drain often belong in the same job here. If a slope is washing out beds, the drainage behind a retaining wall is part of what we build, and we can price the two together. Digging goes faster in a dry stretch, so the work can wait for that window. Because of the drive, send photos of where water pools or runs when it rains, and we will go over them before the walkthrough.

faq.q: How do you choose between a swale and a French drain on a slope?
faq.a: A swale is a shaped, grassed channel that carries surface water around the problem. It works when water runs over the top of the ground. A French drain is for water trapped in the soil. On a hillside we often use both, a swale above the house and a drain where seepage shows up. The written estimate says which and why.

faq.q: What does drainage cost in Nacogdoches?
faq.a: Most projects run $2,000 to $3,750. Small fixes like a downspout reroute or one low spot run $450 to $1,000. A standard single French drain run is $1,900 to $3,000, and full systems run $3,000 to $4,500. Pipe length, dig depth and the outlet set the price. You get it in writing after a walkthrough.

faq.q: Is Nacogdoches too far for a drainage job?
faq.a: Not for a real project. Drainage is one of the jobs we drive down for, along with walls, patios and full landscape installs. A very small single fix may not justify the trip alone, so send your address and photos with a quote request and we will tell you straight.

faq.q: Where does the water go once it leaves my yard?
faq.a: Every drain needs a real outlet. On a hill that is usually daylight lower on your own lot, or a pop-up emitter out in the yard. We do not bury a dead end that backs up the first time the ground saturates. The outlet is named in the estimate before we dig.

faq.q: When is the best time to fix drainage here?
faq.a: We build drains year-round. The best time to see the problem is during or right after a rain, and the best time to dig is a dry stretch, when clay is not saturated. Fixing it before the spring rains means one less season with water against the house.

fertilization.local_h: Why the soil test comes before the bag in Nacogdoches
local: Pine needle duff and acidic rain push Nacogdoches soil low on pH. That is why azaleas, camellias and dogwoods do so well here, and it is also why a lawn can sit there thin no matter how much you feed it. Fertilizer cannot do its job until the pH is corrected. So we test first. If the numbers say lime, lime goes down before anything else, and the plan is written out so you can see the reasoning.

Sometimes the problem is light and not food. On the older streets around downtown and the SFA campus, tall pines and hardwoods shade most of the yard. St. Augustine needs four to five hours of real sun to hold up, and no feeding schedule fixes a lawn that gets less. We look at the shade on the walkthrough and tell you plainly if a shade bed is the smarter answer for that corner.

When a lawn is worth feeding, timing matters more than quantity. The first slow-release feeding goes down once overnight lows hold above 60 and the grass is fully awake. Feed in March and most of it washes out with the next rain. The last real nitrogen goes down in early September, and October is a potassium month, because late nitrogen on St. Augustine feeds large patch. Compacted lawns also get core aeration in late summer.

A full program means four visits spread across the year, and that is hard to run from 70 miles away. What works is a soil test and a corrective feeding set alongside a sod or landscape install, with a written schedule left behind so you or your mower can follow it. If you want to ask about your address, send it with a quote request and we will say what we can take on.

faq.q: Does my Nacogdoches lawn need lime?
faq.a: You cannot tell by looking. Pine needles and acidic rain push local soil low on pH, and low pH holds back what fertilizer can do. A soil test gives the number. If it is low, we add lime to correct it, and the plan we write shows what went down and why.

faq.q: How much does fertilizing cost in Nacogdoches?
faq.a: Feedings start from about $190 per visit. Multi-visit programs are priced on lawn size, the number of rounds, grass type, any lime the test calls for and whether you add core aeration. You get the plan and the price in writing before the first application.

faq.q: Can you put me on the full four-visit program?
faq.a: Usually not as a stand-alone service this far from Longview. Four return trips across the year is not something we can run reliably, and we would rather say so. A test plus a corrective feeding with a new install, and a written schedule for the rest, is the realistic version.

faq.q: When should the first feeding go down?
faq.a: Around the end of April, once overnight lows hold above 60 degrees and the grass is fully awake. March feedings mostly wash out. The last nitrogen goes down in early September, and October gets a low-nitrogen, potassium-heavy winterizer for cold hardiness.

faq.q: Is it worth feeding grass under tall pines?
faq.a: Only if the spot gets enough sun. St. Augustine needs four to five hours. Under a dense canopy with less than that, food will not rescue the lawn, and a bed with shade plants is the better use of the space. We check the light before we quote.

flower-bed-installation.local_h: Beds that fit Nacogdoches light, soil and grade
local: Walk the older blocks near downtown and the SFA campus and you see the usual setup. Tall pines and hardwoods overhead, a bed along the house that gets a few hours of light, and ground that tilts toward the street. Sun annuals stretch and quit in that shade. So the first thing we do is count the hours of sun the bed actually gets, then pick plants for that number and not for the picture on a tag.

Acidic soil is the other half of the picture. Pine needles and rain keep Nacogdoches ground on the acid side, which suits azaleas, camellias, hydrangeas, hollies and ferns. This is the town of the Azalea Trail and the azalea garden at SFA, so you already know what the soil can grow. We save sun-loving color for any spot that gets six hours or more, and we site azaleas and hydrangeas out of the worst afternoon sun.

Slope changes how we build. We cut a clean edge, pull weeds by the root, loosen the top of the soil and work compost into heavy clay. Then we shape the bed so water soaks in instead of running off and washing out the mulch. Plants go in with real spacing so air moves through them, and mulch goes down 1 to 1.5 inches deep, pulled back off the stems.

From 70 miles away, the easy way to start is photos. The $199 Flower Bed Preview works from pictures and rough measurements you send, and the fee is credited toward the install if you book within 90 days. Bigger multi-bed designs and bed work packaged with a landscape install fit the trip best, so mention anything else you are thinking about in the same quote request.

faq.q: Can you plant a bed under my pine trees?
faq.a: Yes, if we choose plants that want shade. Azaleas, camellias, hydrangeas, hollies and ferns handle the light and the acidic soil. In the deepest shade the bed itself may be the best use of the space. We tell you on the walkthrough what each spot can carry.

faq.q: What does a flower bed cost in Nacogdoches?
faq.a: New beds are priced with our planting work, and most projects run $900 to $3,600. A small refresh of an existing bed starts at a few hundred dollars. Bed size, plant count and size, edging material and how much soil prep you need all move the number.

faq.q: Can I see the bed before you build it?
faq.a: Yes. The Flower Bed Preview is $199 and gives you a rendering from photos and measurements. If you book the install within 90 days, the fee is credited toward it. That is an easy way to settle a design when we are 70 miles away.

faq.q: When is the best time to plant?
faq.a: Shrubs and perennials do best in fall, September through November, while the soil is still warm. Heat lovers like vinca should wait until the soil is truly warm, usually mid-May and later. Seasonal color rotates so the bed has something in bloom most of the year.

faq.q: How should I water new plants on a slope?
faq.a: Deep and less often, so roots go down instead of rotting in wet clay. On a slope we shape the bed to hold water long enough to soak in, and we walk you through the schedule when we finish. Daily light watering is how many good plants get killed.

hardscaping.local_h: Putting a flat patio on a Nacogdoches slope
local: Patios and walkways are one of the main reasons we make the drive to Nacogdoches. The town is hillier than most of ours, and few lots hand you a flat spot behind the house. So the build usually starts with a cut. We excavate and level the area, and on steeper ground we add a short seating or retaining wall on the low side to hold the base, rather than hauling in loose fill and hoping.

What sits under the stone matters more than the stone. Much of East Texas is sandy loam over red clay, and the clay swells in a wet spring and shrinks in a dry August. A patio laid on a thin bed of sand will rock and split. We dig to depth, compact a crushed stone base and pitch the surface away from the house so water runs off and not under. On a hill, we plan where that runoff goes before the first paver is set.

We build with concrete pavers, flagstone and chopped stone. Fire pits, seating walls, outdoor kitchens and grill stations can go in the same project, and chopped stone borders hold a field tight. Older lots around downtown and the SFA campus can be tight and shaded, so we look at how material and equipment will get in during the walkthrough. Access is part of the price, and we tell you so in writing.

If you want to see it first, the $449 Hardscape Preview gives you layout renderings from photos and measurements you send. The fee is credited toward the install if you book within 90 days. Base work goes best in a dry stretch, because saturated clay will not compact. Spring and fall book up first, so call a few weeks ahead if you want to be sitting on it by a certain season.

faq.q: Can you build a patio on a steep yard?
faq.a: Yes. We cut and level the area, and on steeper ground add a short retaining or seating wall on the low side to hold the base. Then we compact crushed stone and pitch the surface so water runs away from the house. The walkthrough tells us whether the slope needs more than that.

faq.q: What does a patio cost in Nacogdoches?
faq.a: Most hardscape projects run $3,100 to $9,100. A small patio or walkway lands at the low end and a large outdoor living build costs more. Square footage, the material, how much excavation the site needs, walls and fire features, and access all move the number.

faq.q: Pavers, flagstone or chopped stone?
faq.a: Pavers give a tight, even surface. Flagstone gives a natural, irregular look and works well for paths and stepping stones. Chopped stone suits borders and edging. We will talk you through the tradeoffs on the walkthrough, and the Hardscape Preview can show the layout in each.

faq.q: Will the patio hold up on clay soil?
faq.a: It will if the base is right. The clay moves, so we dig out to the right depth, lay and compact crushed stone, and set the pitch so water sheds away. Where the patio catches roof water or sits at the bottom of a slope, we plan drainage first.

faq.q: Is the drive to Nacogdoches worth it for a patio?
faq.a: Yes, patios and walkways are among the jobs we drive down for. A larger project also lets the same crew stay on the work from the first dig to the last cleanup, and we haul off the spoil when we finish.

hedge-trimming.local_h: Trimming in azalea country without cutting off the bloom
local: Nacogdoches has more azaleas per block than almost anywhere we work. The trouble is that azaleas set next year's flower buds soon after they finish blooming. Trim them in July and you get a green bush with no color the next spring. So we shape azaleas right after the spring show and leave them alone the rest of the year. Older, leggy ones can take a harder cut in that same window, and they take a season to fill back in.

Other shrubs run on a different schedule. Hollies, yaupons and ligustrum get their cut in early summer, after the spring flush hardens off, and they forgive a firm shaping. Boxwood and photinia get the same treatment. If you keep a holly for its winter berries, we go lighter and accept a looser shape. Skip hard shearing in late fall, because the tender regrowth burns brown in the first cold snap.

Hedges under a pine canopy tend to go bare and leggy on the lower branches. We shape each one a little wider at the base than the top so light reaches the lower leaves, and we keep the natural form of the plant instead of boxing everything into the same shape. Foundation shrubs, long screening hedges and formal or topiary work are all part of the job, and so is hard rejuvenation of overgrown plants.

Most hedges want two to three trims a season, and that is the part that is hard to run from Longview. The honest version is that a one-time shaping, paired with mulch, pruning or bed work, is the easy trip. If you want to ask about a recurring schedule, send your address and what you have with a quote request, and we will tell you straight what we can take on.

faq.q: When should azaleas be shaped in Nacogdoches?
faq.a: Right after they finish blooming in spring. They set next year's buds within weeks, so a cut in July or later removes the flowers. Mophead hydrangeas work the same way. Hollies and boxwoods can wait until early summer.

faq.q: How much does hedge trimming cost?
faq.a: Most jobs run $150 to $800. A handful of foundation shrubs sits at the low end, and long, tall or badly overgrown hedges run higher. Shrub count, height, how overgrown they are and how much debris we haul off all matter. You get the price in writing.

faq.q: Can you cut back an overgrown azalea hedge?
faq.a: Yes, in the same post-bloom window. A hard cut on old, leggy azaleas works, but expect a season or so to fill in. We tell you on the walkthrough which plants can take it and which are better replaced.

faq.q: Do you haul away the clippings?
faq.a: Yes. Tarps go down before we start, every clipping is raked up and blown out of the beds, and the debris leaves with us. You are not left with a pile at the curb.

faq.q: Will you trim my hedges on a recurring schedule?
faq.a: We offer two to three trims a season in our core area, but the trip to Nacogdoches makes a recurring schedule hard. Send your address and tell us what you have. We will say honestly what we can take on, and we do not invent a minimum.

irrigation.local_h: Watering a hilly, shaded Nacogdoches yard
local: Nacogdoches lots are hilly, and water on a slope runs off before it soaks in. A system that runs one long cycle floods the low corner and leaves the high side dry. So we zone slopes on their own and run shorter cycles, giving water time to sink in between runs. The sand on top takes water fast, but the clay under it stops it, so short and repeated beats long and heavy.

Sun and shade get their own zones too. Under the pines and hardwoods on the older streets near downtown and the SFA campus, St. Augustine needs less water than the Bermuda out on an open, sunny lot. We lay out heads for full coverage on turf and keep the plan separate for each kind of ground. Every zone is run and adjusted for coverage before we call it done.

Beds go on drip. Spray heads in a bed wet the leaves, the mulch and the side of the house and still leave the roots thirsty. Drip puts the water where azaleas, camellias and hydrangeas need it and keeps foliage dry, which matters for fungus in a warm, humid spring. A system tied to city water gets a backflow prevention device, and new automatic systems get a rain or freeze sensor.

Texas treats irrigation as licensed work, so the design and install run under a Texas licensed irrigator, who checks the system. Many East Texas cities require a permit for a new system, and the rules vary. We check what your address requires and pull it before we dig. Because of the distance, we take new installs here, and the free walkthrough is where we settle the zones, the water source and the price. Send photos of the yard and the spot where your water line comes in with the quote request, and we will bring questions instead of guesses.

faq.q: Are you licensed to install sprinklers in Nacogdoches?
faq.a: Yes. Our irrigation work is designed and installed under a Texas licensed irrigator, who checks every system. We pull the permits the job requires. Nacogdoches is outside our home county, so we confirm what your address needs before we start.

faq.q: How much does a sprinkler system cost?
faq.a: It depends on the size of the area, the number of zones, turf heads versus bed drip, your water source and pressure, and slopes and trees. We price irrigation after a free walkthrough and send a written, itemized quote.

faq.q: Can you fix a system I already have?
faq.a: Heads, lines, valves and wiring are part of our irrigation work. From 70 miles out, though, we mostly take scheduled projects and not small service calls. Send your address and what the system is doing, and we will tell you straight what we can take.

faq.q: Should my beds be on drip or spray?
faq.a: Drip, almost always. Spray heads in a bed waste water to wind and evaporation and soak the leaves and the house. Drip puts water at the roots and keeps foliage dry. We run beds on drip and keep turf on its own zones.

faq.q: When is the best time to put in a system?
faq.a: Spring or fall, when the ground is workable and the lawn recovers fast from trenching. Before the first hard freeze, make sure the freeze sensor works or the system is shut off, and check every zone again when you turn it back on.

landscaping.local_h: Planning a landscape around Nacogdoches pines and hills
local: A landscape here starts with the canopy. Tall pines and hardwoods shade much of the town near downtown and the SFA campus, and the ground tilts toward La Nana and Banita creeks. We walk the property, note where the sun falls in summer and where water runs after a rain, and lay out beds from that. The plant list leans on what likes shade and acid: azaleas, camellias, hollies and ferns, with heat-tough color saved for the sunny spots.

You can see what the soil grows at the SFA Gardens and the Ruby M. Mize Azalea Garden. We plant for the same ground. Trees and shrubs go in with the root flare at grade and native soil backfilled around them, and not a pocket of bagged mix that holds water like a bathtub. Beds get edged, weeds pulled by the root, heavy clay amended with compost and a finish of mulch or rock.

leaf-removal.local_h: What falls on a Nacogdoches lot, and what it does to the lawn
local: Tall pines and hardwoods shade much of the older town, and that canopy drops something all winter. Pine needles come down year-round and heavily in fall. Hardwoods let go of leaves from October into February. On the streets near downtown and the SFA campus, the leaf layer can be deep by Thanksgiving. We time any cleanup to what is actually on the ground in your lot, not to a date on a calendar.

Wet leaves on shaded St. Augustine through winter are how lawns come up dead in spring. St. Augustine grows from surface runners and stays partly green into November, so every growing point sits right where the leaves land. A wet mat plus mild fall nights sets up large patch, and in March the owner finds dead circles and blames the cold. Often it was the leaves. Count a heavy November leaf cover as urgent, not cosmetic.

A visit works like this. The crew blows leaves and needles out of the lawn, the shrub beds and the rock beds onto the street or another paved surface. We run the leaf vacuum trailer, which shreds about 10 yards of leaves down to 1, and haul it all away. We clear the driveway, walks and patio, re-edge bed lines the leaves buried, and can clear the gutters too. Nothing gets bagged.

Recurring passes through the whole fall are hard to run from Longview. A big one-time cleanup, especially with mulch, bed work or pruning in the same trip, is the version that can be worth the drive. Send the address, the lot size and a photo of the canopy with a quote request. We will tell you honestly whether it works, and the flat price comes in writing before we start.

faq.q: Can you do a one-time leaf cleanup in Nacogdoches?

faq.q: Why are leaves on St. Augustine such a problem?
faq.a: St. Augustine stays green longer and grows from surface runners, so a wet leaf mat smothers it and feeds large patch. Bermuda goes dormant early, so leaves on it are mostly just unsightly. Shaded St. Augustine under oaks and pines is the lawn that pays.

faq.q: When should the cleanup happen?
faq.a: Plan on the first half of November, when sweetgums and other hardwoods let go and volume jumps. Post oaks and water oaks keep dropping into February, so a second pass in December and a last one before spring green-up are common.

mulch-installation.local_h: Pine straw or hardwood on a Nacogdoches bed
local: Under Nacogdoches pines, beds collect a layer of needles every year, and pine straw is a fine mulch on its own. It fits the look under pines, suits acid-loving shrubs like azaleas and camellias, and it holds well on a slope, where the needles knit together and stay put. Pine straw is available on request, and we match what is already in the bed so it breaks down evenly.

Where you want a cleaner, darker look, we go with shredded hardwood, which breaks down into the soil as it ages. Cypress breaks down slower, and dyed black or brown gives more contrast. Whichever you pick, we start with the bed. The edge is re-cut so grass cannot creep in, every weed is pulled by the root because mulch hides weeds and does not kill them, and the crusted top inch of soil is loosened.

Then comes depth. Every online calculator says three inches, and that number comes from snow country. Here, three inches sheds light rain like a tarp and holds moisture against stems until they rot. We lay 1 to 1.5 inches, raked even and pulled back off stems and trunks, and we never put fabric underneath. Mulch is supposed to turn into soil, and fabric stops that.

Late April through mid-May is the best window, right after the spring growth flush. The second is late September through October, when a thin top-dress goes down before the leaves drop. From 70 miles away, mulch is easiest to fit in with bed installs, hedge shaping or a landscape project. Send photos of the beds with a quote request, and we will tell you straight whether it works as a stand-alone trip.

faq.q: Pine straw or hardwood mulch in Nacogdoches?
faq.a: Both work. Pine straw fits under pines, suits acid-loving plants and holds on slopes. Hardwood gives a darker, cleaner look and builds the soil as it breaks down. Either way we skip landscape fabric and keep it off stems and trunks.

faq.q: How much does a mulch refresh cost?
faq.a: Most beds run $600 to $2,400. The price follows the bed square footage, the number of beds, the mulch type, how much edging and weed pulling is needed and whether it is a full install or a thin top-dress.

faq.q: Why only 1 to 1.5 inches?
faq.a: Deeper mulch sheds light rain, holds heat and moisture against stems and gives voles cover to eat roots. We do not get snow loads here, so there is nothing to pack it down. A prepared bed with 1 to 1.5 inches works better and costs less.

faq.q: Can you just top-dress my beds in the fall?
faq.a: Yes. A thin top-dress goes down in late September through October, before the leaves drop, and costs a fraction of a full install if the old layer is still there. We measure the beds so you only pay for what they need.

faq.q: Is mulch worth the trip to Nacogdoches?

retaining-walls.local_h: Holding a Nacogdoches hillside in place
local: Plenty of Nacogdoches yards slope hard toward the street or down toward a creek. Rain runs off those slopes fast, strips soil from the beds and leaves a yard you cannot really use. A retaining wall fixes that in two ways. It flattens a strip of ground for a lawn, a patio or a play area, and it holds the soil that was washing away. Terraced walls step down a steeper grade in stages.

Most walls that fail in East Texas fail from water. Clay swells when wet and shrinks when dry, and behind a wall that water has nowhere to go. It builds pressure until the wall leans, bows and cracks. On a hill that sheds water from above, the risk is higher. So behind every wall we put a gravel chimney and a perforated drain tied out to daylight or a pop-up emitter, so pressure never builds.

Below the wall, the base does the work. Sandy loam over clay will not hold a wall set on undisturbed dirt. We dig below grade, compact a crushed stone base and set the first course dead level, because every row above inherits it. Taller walls get geogrid tied back into the hill and a slight lean into the slope. We build in segmental block, natural stone, boulders and pressure-treated timber, and we rebuild leaning walls.

Height drives the plan. A wall over about four feet usually needs engineered design, and we say so at the walkthrough if your slope calls for a stamped plan. Wall and drainage often go in together, and so do a patio or planting above the wall. Dry weather is best for digging, but a leaning wall should not wait for the spring rains. Send photos of the slope with a quote request.

faq.q: How much does a retaining wall cost in Nacogdoches?
faq.a: Most walls run $3,000 to $19,000 by height and length. Short garden walls start at a few thousand dollars, and tall structural walls run $20,000 and up. Block or stone, excavation, drainage and geogrid also move the number. You get it in writing after a walkthrough.

faq.q: How tall a wall can you build?
faq.a: From short garden and seating walls to tall structural walls. Over about four feet usually means engineered design and geogrid, and we tell you at the walkthrough if your slope needs a stamped plan.

faq.q: Can you fix a wall that is leaning?
faq.a: Yes. Rebuilding leaning or failed walls is part of the service. Usually the cause is water and a weak base, so we rebuild course by course on a compacted base with gravel and a drain behind it. Do not wait for the spring rains to make it worse.

faq.q: What material should the wall be?
faq.a: Segmental block gives a clean, even look. Natural stone and boulders suit a more rustic yard. Pressure-treated timber works for lower walls. Height, budget and how the wall meets the house decide it, and we go over the options at the walkthrough.

faq.q: Is Nacogdoches too far for a wall?
faq.a: No. Walls are one of the main jobs we drive down for. The same crew stays through the dig, the base and the finish, and we haul off the spoil. Photos of the slope sent with your quote request help us come prepared.

sod-installation.local_h: Choosing the right grass under Nacogdoches pines
local: Under the pines and oaks that shade the older streets, St. Augustine is the only common lawn grass that holds on. Bermuda needs six to eight hours of direct sun, and in shade it thins to dirt by August. St. Augustine holds on with four to six hours. Under about four hours, no turf lasts long, and that spot is better turned into a bed. We map the sun on the walkthrough before we price anything.

On open, sunny lots and slopes, Bermuda is the pick. It roots in and holds the soil, which matters on a hill where water runs off fast. We usually lay Tif419 for sun. For shade it is St. Augustine in Floratam, Palmetto or Raleigh, depending on how much shade tolerance the spot needs. Many Nacogdoches yards should be split, Bermuda in the open front and St. Augustine under the trees out back.

The prep is what makes sod take. We strip the old turf and weeds down to bare soil, regrade where water needs to move, and till in two to three inches of compost or topsoil. Acidic soil in this area makes a soil test worth doing before starter fertilizer goes down. Then we level and roll the bed, lay the sod with staggered seams and no gaps, and set a written watering schedule.

Timing is firm. Bermuda goes down from late April through August, and St. Augustine from May through September, with a deadline near the end of September so it has four to six weeks of root growth before dormancy. New sod needs a deep morning soak every day for the first two weeks. A full-yard install is a project the crew finishes in one stretch, which is why the drive makes sense.

faq.q: Will sod grow under my pine trees?
faq.a: St. Augustine can, if the spot gets four to five hours of real sun. Under a dense canopy with less, nothing holds for long. We look at the light before we quote and will say if a shade bed is the smarter move.

faq.q: How much does sod cost in Nacogdoches?
faq.a: Sod is priced by the pallet based on the square footage, and most projects run $1,500 to $4,700. Small patch repairs cost less. Grass type, removal of old turf, grading and soil work, drainage and pallet access all move the number.

faq.q: Bermuda or St. Augustine for my lot?
faq.a: Sun decides. Bermuda wants six to eight hours of direct sun and does well on open lots and slopes. St. Augustine tolerates shade and covers most older, wooded lots. A lot of yards need both, and we split them.

faq.q: When should sod go down?
faq.a: Bermuda from late April through August, St. Augustine from May through September. Get St. Augustine in by the end of September so it has four to six weeks of roots before dormancy. Laid in November, it sits on the ground like a rug.

faq.q: What does watering look like after install?
faq.a: A daily morning soak for the first two weeks, then a taper to deep, less frequent watering as the roots take hold. We give you the schedule in writing. Skipping those first two weeks in summer heat can brown out a new install.

tree-planting.local_h: Fitting a new tree into a Nacogdoches yard
local: The first question in Nacogdoches is what light the spot gets. Under the pine canopy near downtown and the SFA campus, understory trees fit best. Redbuds and dogwoods work at the edge of the pines. Live oaks and Shumard oaks need open ground and room to spread, so they belong on the open lots. We look at sun, drainage, nearby structures and the mature size before we name a species.

Planting depth kills more new trees than anything else. We set the root flare, where the trunk widens into its first roots, at grade or an inch above, and on container trees that flare is often buried a few inches under the potting soil. The hole is two to three times the width of the root ball and no deeper than the ball is tall. Native soil goes back in, since a pocket of bagged soil in clay holds water like a bathtub.

Hills change the finish. On a slope we set the tree so the flare sits at grade and build a low berm on the downhill side, so water soaks into the root ball and does not run past it. A wide mulch ring, pulled back off the trunk, keeps soil from washing. We cut circling roots, build a watering basin, and stake only on windy, exposed sites.

We plant October through February in Nacogdoches, so roots settle in before summer. A tree set in October gets close to six months of root growth before the heat, while one planted in April gets about eight weeks. The new tree drinks from its root ball until roots reach native soil, so we leave a written watering plan, and on bigger installs we check back around the 30-day mark.

faq.q: Can you plant trees on a sloped lot?
faq.a: Yes. We set the root flare at grade, build a low berm on the downhill side so water soaks in, and lay a wide mulch ring to hold the soil. We plant in fall and winter so roots establish before summer.

faq.q: What does tree planting cost?
faq.a: We do not publish a price because the tree itself drives most of the cost. Species, size at planting, the number of trees, access and soil and drainage at the spot all matter. You get a written quote, with the aftercare plan, after a walkthrough.

faq.q: Which trees work under the pines?
faq.a: Redbuds and dogwoods work as understory trees at the edge of the pines. Live oaks and Shumard oaks need open ground and room to spread. We will tell you on the walkthrough which spots can carry which tree.

faq.q: How often should I water a new tree?
faq.a: Soak the root ball with a hose on a trickle for about twenty minutes. For a fall tree, do it twice a week for six weeks, then weekly through November, then every ten to fourteen days in a dry winter. Soak it the day before a hard freeze.

faq.q: Is it worth the trip for one tree?
faq.a: Trees pair best with a landscape install, where the crew is already on site. For a single tree, send photos and your address with a quote request. We will tell you honestly whether we can take it and will not make up a minimum.

tree-shrub-care.local_h: Pruning on the right schedule under a Nacogdoches canopy
local: Plant a dogwood, an azalea, a camellia and a crepe myrtle in the same bed and you have four different pruning calendars. That is a normal older Nacogdoches yard, usually under a tall pine canopy. Azaleas and camellias get cut right after they bloom. Crepe myrtles are thinned in February while dormant. Hollies and boxwoods go in early summer. Each plant gets cut at the branch collar, sized to what it can close.

Crepe myrtles are where most damage happens. Topping them into stumps makes the tree grow back taller on weaker wood. We thin instead, taking out crossing and rubbing branches and limbing the tree up so the bark shows. A topped tree can be brought back over two or three winters, and we plan that out. If the tree is wrong for the spot, the answer is a smaller variety and not a saw.

Pines and hardwoods drop limbs, and dead lower branches shade the lawn and hang over beds. We clear dead lower limbs off shade trees, remove small trees and overgrown shrubs so light reaches the beds, and haul off every limb. Oaks are pruned in the dead of winter or the heat of late summer, because the beetles that spread oak wilt are drawn to fresh cuts in spring and early summer.

Big pines and hardwoods near a house call for a tree service with the right equipment, and we will tell you when that is the case. Our part is the pruning, shaping and cleanup that keeps the rest of the yard healthy. Send photos of what you have with a quote request, and we will say honestly whether the trip makes sense. A pruning visit pairs well with a mulch refresh around the tree bases, and seasonal feeding for trees and shrubs can go in the same trip.

faq.q: Do you remove trees in Nacogdoches?
faq.a: We remove small trees and overgrown shrubs as part of pruning and cleanup. Big pines and hardwoods near a house need a tree service with the right equipment, and we will say so on the walkthrough.

faq.q: When should I prune crepe myrtles?
faq.a: In February, while they are dormant and before the buds break. We thin them and do not top them. Topping makes the tree grow back taller on weaker wood. If one was topped for years, we bring it back over two or three winters.

faq.q: When do azaleas and camellias get pruned?
faq.a: Right after they bloom in spring, since they set next year's buds soon after. A cut later in the year removes the flowers. We schedule these first and leave the plants alone after that.

faq.q: Why are oaks pruned in winter or late summer?
faq.a: Oak wilt spreads partly through beetles drawn to fresh sap at a cut, and they are most active in spring and early summer. We avoid that window. If a storm breaks a limb, we cut it clean and seal the wound right away.

faq.q: How much does tree and shrub care cost?
faq.a: We do not publish a price. It depends on how many trees and shrubs, their size and condition, whether it is light shaping or recovery pruning, small removals and haul-off. You get a written, itemized quote after a free walkthrough.
